summary: Offshore light (1934-35) marking the channel into Green Bay, Wisconsin; manned by keepers, then Coast Guard crews from 1939; automated 1979-80.

structures.type: cylindrical concrete pier on a timber and concrete crib
steel light tower on a steel service building
structures.note: tower about 30 ft tall (NRHP); about 95 ft from foundation base to top of lantern (NRHP)

facts.fog_signal: air-powered diaphragm horn in 1935; now an automated fog signal (NRHP)

events.note: Lighthouse Board sent a group to Green Bay to choose sites: Grassy Island, Peshtigo Reef, Chambers Island.
Congress appropriated $25,000 for light stations at the three sites; appropriation withdrawn 1867; only Chambers Island was built.
Construction began with a wooden crib.
Pier towed out and sunk on 5 June 1935 (LighthouseFriends). Construction completed and station formally established in 1935 (NRHP).
Began operating in 1935 (NRHP). No exact first-lighting date in the sources read.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens in the lantern, with a 5,000 candlepower lamp (NRHP). LighthouseFriends gives 6,000 candlepower.
Bureau of Lighthouses merged into the Coast Guard; station then manned by Coast Guard personnel on two-week rotations during the shipping season (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).

Head keeper Theodore Grosskopf and three men stranded in December by bad weather; supplies dropped by plane; rescued over the ice by John Paetschow and three Coast Guardsmen. LighthouseFriends is the only source read.
Distance-finding station discontinued 'in the 1950s' (NRHP); exact year not given.
Radiobeacon discontinued; steel antenna tower on the lantern remains (NRHP).

corrections.why: The record's green characteristic conflicts with both the 2008 nomination (a red light) and LighthouseFriends (an occulting red light with a four-second period). The nomination's 1935 description, a red light of 4 s on and 2 s dark, gives a six-second cycle, so the period itself is disputed. A human should check the current Light List entry before the value changes.

notes_for_editor: Roster matched by name only: the USLHS place record gives no position for this station, so the match is by name and not checked against location. The archive keeps the title 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper' for its heads through 1974, while the nomination and LighthouseFriends describe Coast Guard crews of two weeks on and two weeks off from 1939; the sources do not reconcile and the story says so. Characteristic: record Fl G 6s; nomination red (1935: 4 s on, 2 s dark; winter: 1 s flash in 10 s); LighthouseFriends 1935 fixed red at 6,000 cp, and today an occulting red light with a four-second period. The story states that the 1935 descriptions disagree. Automation year: NRHP 1980, LighthouseFriends 1979. Range: NRHP says 'visible for 12 miles in clear weather' with no nautical qualifier; the record's range_nm 10.4 was not sourced and is removed. Lighting date for 1935 not given in any source read. Chronicling America searches (Grosskopf with Green Bay, 1943; Green Bay with lighthouse and coast guard, 1943-44) returned no Wisconsin pages, so the December 1943 stranding rests on LighthouseFriends alone. The 1959 Appleton Post-Crescent article itself was not read; the account is LighthouseFriends' and the story says so only through its sourcing. The 1937 Lighthouse Service Bulletin mentions Green Bay among stations that have proven useful, but the OCR is too garbled to quote, so it is not cited. The 1917 Commissioner entry for 'West Bank, Green Bay Harbor' is a different aid and is not used. LighthouseFriends gives a total cost of $108,447 for the station; not used, as it rests on that one page. LighthouseFriends' roster dates differ from the USLHS place record in places (for example McFarlin 1959-1960 against -1960); the USLHS record is kept. The record has no access field; the nomination says accessible by boat.
